days.title: Day 12 – Advanced Functions and Closures
days.definition: Advanced functions include concepts like closures, higher-order functions, function currying, and recursion that enable powerful programming patterns.

explanation.main: Understanding advanced function concepts is crucial for writing efficient and maintainable JavaScript code.
key_points: Closures: Functions that remember their lexical scope
Higher-order functions: Functions that take other functions as arguments or return functions
Currying: Transforming a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions
Recursion: Functions that call themselves with modified parameters
Memoization: Caching function results for optimization

days.real_world_example: Closures are used in module patterns, private variables, and event handlers. Higher-order functions power array methods like map, filter, and reduce. Currying enables function specialization in libraries like Lodash. Recursion processes nested data structures. Memoization optimizes expensive calculations.
interactive_tasks: Create a closure-based counter with increment/decrement
Implement a memoized Fibonacci function
Build a curry function that handles variable arguments
Create a higher-order function that logs execution time

quiz.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
options: A function that remembers its lexical scope
A function that returns another function
quiz.answer: A function that remembers its lexical scope
quiz.reasoning: A closure gives you access to an outer function's scope from an inner function.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of memoization?
quiz.reasoning: Memoization stores the results of expensive function calls and returns cached result when same inputs occur.

quiz.question: What is function currying?
options: Transforming a function to take multiple arguments one at a time
quiz.answer: Transforming a function to take multiple arguments one at a time
quiz.reasoning: Currying transforms a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions each with single argument.

days.title: Day 13 – Prototypes and Inheritance
days.definition: JavaScript uses prototypal inheritance where objects can inherit properties and methods from other objects through prototype chains.

explanation.main: Understanding prototypes is essential for working with JavaScript's object-oriented features.
key_points: Every JavaScript object has a prototype property
Prototype chain allows inheritance of properties and methods
Constructor functions create objects with shared prototype
ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes
Object.create() creates objects with specified prototype
Instance vs prototype properties

days.real_world_example: Prototypal inheritance is used in JavaScript frameworks, custom class hierarchies, library development, and when extending built-in objects. Most JavaScript frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) use prototypes internally for component inheritance.
interactive_tasks: Create a Shape hierarchy with Circle and Rectangle inheriting from Shape
Implement a custom Array class with additional methods
Build a Vehicle class hierarchy with Car, Bike, and Truck
Create a mixin pattern using Object.assign() with prototypes

quiz.question: What is the prototype chain in JavaScript?
options: A series of parent objects that properties are inherited from
quiz.answer: A series of parent objects that properties are inherited from
quiz.reasoning: When accessing a property, JavaScript looks up the prototype chain until it finds the property or reaches null.

quiz.question: What does the 'new' keyword do?
options: Creates a new object and sets its prototype
quiz.answer: Creates a new object and sets its prototype
quiz.reasoning: The 'new' keyword creates a new object, sets its prototype to the constructor's prototype, and calls the constructor with 'this' bound to the new object.

quiz.question: How do ES6 classes relate to prototypes?
options: They are syntactic sugar over prototypes
They have no relation to prototypes
quiz.answer: They are syntactic sugar over prototypes
quiz.reasoning: ES6 classes provide a cleaner syntax for creating constructor functions and prototypes but work the same way under the hood.

days.title: Day 14 – Error Handling and Debugging
days.definition: Error handling involves catching and managing runtime errors, while debugging is the process of finding and fixing bugs in code.

explanation.main: Proper error handling makes applications more robust and debugging helps identify issues efficiently.
key_points: try-catch-finally blocks for error handling
Throwing custom errors with Error objects
Error types: SyntaxError, ReferenceError, TypeError, etc.
Debugging tools: console methods, debugger statement, browser dev tools
Error propagation in async code
Best practices for error messages and logging

days.real_world_example: Error handling is crucial for form validation, API calls, file operations, and user input processing. Debugging techniques are used daily by developers to fix bugs, optimize performance, and understand code flow. Production applications use error tracking services like Sentry or LogRocket.
interactive_tasks: Create a robust validation function with custom error types
Implement a retry mechanism for failed API calls
Build a debug logging utility with different log levels
Create error boundary component for frontend applications

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 'finally' block in try-catch?
options: To execute code regardless of try/catch outcome
quiz.answer: To execute code regardless of try/catch outcome
quiz.reasoning: The finally block executes after try and catch blocks, regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught.

quiz.question: Which console method is useful for measuring code performance?
quiz.reasoning: console.time() starts a timer and console.timeEnd() stops it, logging the elapsed time.

quiz.question: What does the 'debugger' statement do?
options: Pauses execution if dev tools are open
quiz.answer: Pauses execution if dev tools are open
quiz.reasoning: The debugger statement invokes any available debugging functionality, typically pausing execution and opening dev tools.

days.title: Day 15 – Modules and Code Organization
days.definition: JavaScript modules allow you to split code into separate files that can be imported and exported, promoting better code organization and reusability.

explanation.main: Modules help manage complexity in large applications by separating concerns and dependencies.
key_points: ES6 modules use import/export syntax
Named exports vs default exports
Module bundlers (Webpack, Rollup, Parcel) for production
CommonJS (require/module.exports) used in Node.js
Tree shaking for eliminating unused code
Circular dependency management
Dynamic imports for code splitting

days.real_world_example: Modern web applications use modules to organize code into components, services, utilities, and features. Frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular heavily rely on modules. Build tools like Webpack and Vite bundle modules for production. Node.js uses CommonJS modules. Large codebases use modules to separate concerns and improve maintainability.
interactive_tasks: Create a math utility module with various functions
Build a user management module with CRUD operations
Implement a module bundler simulation
Create a plugin system using modules

quiz.question: What is the difference between named and default exports?
options: Named exports can be multiple, default is one per module
quiz.answer: Named exports can be multiple, default is one per module
quiz.reasoning: A module can have multiple named exports but only one default export.

quiz.question: What is tree shaking?
quiz.reasoning: Tree shaking removes unused code (dead code) from the final bundle, reducing file size.

quiz.question: What are dynamic imports useful for?
quiz.reasoning: Dynamic imports allow loading modules on demand, improving initial load time by splitting code.

days.title: Day 17 – Web APIs and Browser APIs
days.definition: Web APIs provide interfaces to interact with browser features and web platform capabilities beyond the core JavaScript language.

explanation.main: Browser APIs extend JavaScript's capabilities with web-specific functionality.
key_points: DOM APIs: document, window, navigator, location, history
Storage APIs: localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB
Fetch API: modern replacement for XMLHttpRequest
Canvas API: 2D drawing and animation
Geolocation API: access device location
Web Workers: run scripts in background threads
Service Workers: proxy for network requests
Media APIs: audio, video, getUserMedia

days.real_world_example: Web APIs power modern web applications: localStorage for offline data, Fetch API for API calls, Canvas for charts and games, Geolocation for maps, Web Workers for heavy computations without blocking UI, Service Workers for offline capabilities, and Media APIs for video/audio applications.
interactive_tasks: Build a simple drawing application with Canvas API
Create an offline-first app with localStorage and Service Workers
Implement a location-based weather app
Build a file uploader with drag-and-drop API

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of Web Workers?
options: They run JavaScript in background threads
quiz.answer: They run JavaScript in background threads
quiz.reasoning: Web Workers run scripts in background threads, preventing heavy computations from blocking the UI.

quiz.question: What's the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
options: localStorage persists, sessionStorage clears on tab close
quiz.answer: localStorage persists, sessionStorage clears on tab close
quiz.reasoning: localStorage data persists until explicitly cleared, sessionStorage data clears when page session ends (tab closed).

quiz.question: What does the Fetch API replace?
quiz.reasoning: Fetch API is modern replacement for XMLHttpRequest for making HTTP requests.
